samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-10-29 to 2024-01-14. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On October 2, 2023, the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) issued a forecast predicting that high tides, not directly associated with a major storm, were likely to cause coastal flooding in several areas of the U.S., particularly along the eastern seaboard, from October 27-31, 2023. The prediction highlighted specific locations in the Southeast, including Savannah (Fort Pulaski), Georgia; Charleston and Myrtle Beach, South Carolina; and several locations on Florida's Atlantic coast such as Miami, Cape Canaveral, and Fernandina Beach. The forecast, based on a model including tide predictions and sea level trends, noted that real-time weather conditions could alter the outcome. The increased likelihood of flooding during this period was attributed to the occurrence of perigean spring tides combined with seasonally higher mean sea levels. <2> A state of emergency was declared in New York City and surrounding areas after the remnants of Tropical Storm Ophelia stalled over the region on September 29, 2023, causing significant and life-threatening flash flooding. The storm system brought torrential downpours, with some parts of Brooklyn receiving over eight inches of rain, and John F. Kennedy International Airport recording its wettest day since 1948. The intense rainfall, which followed an already wet month, overwhelmed the city's infrastructure, leading to widespread disruptions. Major subway lines and commuter rails, including Metro-North, were suspended or severely delayed, stranding commuters. Flooding also forced the closure of a terminal at LaGuardia Airport, led to flight cancellations and delays at all three area airports, and inundated major roadways, with drivers abandoning vehicles on highways like the FDR Drive. The flooding impacted schools, forced evacuations, and resulted in numerous water rescues. <3> On September 29, 2023, a stalled low-pressure system that had absorbed the remnants of Tropical Storm Ophelia caused major flooding across the New York metropolitan area. The resulting torrential rainfall prompted New York Governor Kathy Hochul to declare a state of emergency. The event led to widespread, severe disruptions; a terminal at LaGuardia Airport was closed, service was suspended on multiple lines of the Metro-North Railroad and the New York City Subway, and numerous schools and businesses, including several Alamo Drafthouse cinemas, were forced to close. John F. Kennedy International Airport recorded 8.65 inches of rain, making it the airport's wettest day since 1948 and the highest September rainfall in a 24-hour period since Hurricane Donna in 1960. With a total of 14.25 inches of rain for the month, September 2023 became the second-rainiest September in New York City since records began, surpassed only by the 16.85 inches recorded in September 1882. <4> On September 11, 2023, a slow-moving storm system resulted in catastrophic flash flooding in Leominster, Massachusetts, after dropping nearly 10 to 11 inches of rain in just a few hours. The deluge caused significant damage, including the collapse of buildings, the formation of sinkholes, and forced evacuations. One major concern was the Barrett Park Pond Dam, which was compromised, prompting precautionary evacuations for residents in low-lying areas nearby. Governor Maura Healey toured the affected areas on September 12 and declared a state of emergency for Leominster and North Attleborough, which also suffered extensive flooding with damage to about 200 homes. The broader storm system impacted not only other parts of Massachusetts but also Rhode Island and Connecticut between September 8 and September 13, 2023. <5> In late August 2023, Hurricane Idalia formed from a tropical depression on August 26 and rapidly intensified over the Gulf of Mexico, briefly becoming a Category 4 storm. [3] On August 30, 2023, Idalia made landfall near Keaton Beach in Florida's Big Bend region as a high-end Category 3 hurricane with winds of 125 mph. [7, 9, 15] The hurricane brought a catastrophic storm surge of 7 to 12 feet to coastal communities in Taylor and Dixie Counties, with Cedar Key experiencing record-high water levels. [6, 7, 8] After making landfall, Idalia moved across northern Florida and into southeast Georgia while still a hurricane, before weakening to a tropical storm as it tracked through South and North Carolina on August 30-31. [3, 4, 13] The storm caused significant and widespread power outages, affecting nearly half a million customers in Florida and Georgia alone. [9, 10] Heavy rainfall was widespread, with localized totals exceeding 10 inches, leading to significant flash flooding in inland communities across Florida, Georgia, and the Carolinas. [8, 13, 15] Coastal cities in the Carolinas, including Charleston, also experienced major flooding from storm surge. [8, 18] <6> A potent summer rainstorm on August 23, 2023, resulted in significant flash flooding along the Las Vegas Strip. The storm, which began in the late evening, turned parts of Las Vegas Boulevard into what appeared to be a river, with floodwaters rushing down the street. The heavy rainfall caused damage to at least one casino; at Harrah's Las Vegas, some ceiling tiles were damaged and water leaked onto the casino floor, though the roof did not collapse and only minor repairs were needed. The Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department received multiple reports of individuals caught in drainage channels starting around 8:56 p.m. In response, the Clark County Fire Department conducted rescue operations, assisting at least one person out of the water while searching for others who were reportedly swept away. Subsequent searches by ground and air for other missing persons did not locate any additional victims. <7> On August 20, 2023, the remnants of Hurricane Hilary delivered significant rainfall and flooding to Southern California and its desert regions. [1, 2] The event was notable for prompting the first-ever tropical storm watches and warnings in California. [3, 4] While Hilary made landfall in Baja California, Mexico, as a tropical storm and was initially reported to have maintained that status upon entering the U.S., a subsequent post-storm analysis by the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA) National Hurricane Center concluded otherwise. [1, 5] The final report determined that Hilary had degenerated into a post-tropical low over northern Baja California before crossing into California. [2, 5] Despite the reclassification, the storm's impact remained significant, causing life-threatening flooding and damage across the region. [1, 5] <8> On July 19, 2023, a series of slow-moving thunderstorms caused historic flash flooding across western Kentucky and parts of southern Illinois. Rainfall totals in the region reached between 10 and 12 inches. Specifically, the city of Mayfield in Graves County, Kentucky, recorded 11.28 inches of rain in a 24-hour period. This amount was noted as a potential new state record, pending official confirmation, which would surpass the 10.48 inches recorded in Louisville on March 1, 1997. The catastrophic flooding prompted Kentucky's governor to declare a state of emergency, leading to numerous water rescues and causing significant damage to infrastructure and property. <9> On Saturday, July 15, 2023, a sudden and catastrophic flash flood occurred in Upper Makefield Township, Bucks County, Pennsylvania, after an intense rainstorm deluged the area. [2, 3] The storm, which began around 5:00 PM local time, dropped an estimated 6.5 to 7 inches of rain in under an hour, with some sources specifying the duration as 45 minutes. [2] The torrent overwhelmed local streams and drainage systems, sweeping away multiple vehicles. [2] The event resulted in six confirmed fatalities and a 9-month-old boy who was presumed dead; his mother and 2-year-old sister were among the deceased. [1] Initial reports had confirmed three to five deaths while search efforts continued for the missing children. [2, 3] The flood caused significant damage to homes, businesses, roads, and bridges, with officials describing it as a new benchmark for severe weather in the area, surpassing the devastation of Hurricane Ida in 2021. [2] <10> On July 9, 2023, Berks County, Pennsylvania, experienced a severe weather event characterized by historic flash flooding and excessive rainfall. The National Weather Service reported rainfall totals of 5.35 inches in the city of Reading and as high as 6.69 inches in West Lawn. Some local reports indicated totals nearing 7 inches in certain areas. The torrential rain led to widespread, dangerous flash flooding, trapping residents in homes and vehicles and prompting numerous water rescues by emergency responders, including the National Guard. Significant damage occurred throughout the region, notably impacting Muhlenberg Township and causing the loss of a building at Antietam High School. While the event was described as a "100-year storm" by local officials, a subsequent request for a federal major disaster declaration from FEMA was denied.

Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A complex storm system generated catastrophic flash flooding in Roswell and Chaves County, New Mexico, on October 19, 2024. [5, 7, 8] On that day, Roswell recorded an all-time high of 5.78 inches of rain, a figure representing nearly half of its average annual precipitation and surpassing the 500-year storm threshold according to NOAA Atlas 14. [4] The resulting life-threatening floods led to over 300 water rescues, nearly 40 hospitalizations, and two confirmed fatalities. [5, 7, 10] The severe weather inundated homes and businesses, swept away vehicles, and caused significant damage to local infrastructure. [4, 8] <2> A NOAA forecast predicted coastal flooding would impact the U.S. beginning on October 18, 2024, due to a perigean spring tide, where the full moon coincides with its closest point to Earth. [9] In the Northeast, a Coastal Flood Advisory was issued for eastern Massachusetts, Cape Cod, and the Islands for October 18, with an offshore coastal storm contributing to minor flooding. [8] News reports confirmed that areas of Boston's waterfront experienced flooding from the "supermoon" high tide. [3] Portland and Providence were part of a broader NOAA outlook but not included in the specific NWS advisory provided. [8, 9] Concurrently, the National Weather Service issued a Coastal Flooding Statement for all coastal areas of Hawaii's Big Island, warning of potential flooding from October 18 through October 20 due to higher-than-normal tides. [7] <3> On October 17, 2024, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center released its U.S. Winter Outlook for the period of December 2024 through February 2025. The forecast predicts wetter-than-average conditions across the northern tier of the continental United States, with the highest probabilities in the Pacific Northwest and the Great Lakes region. This weather pattern is attributed to a slowly-developing La Niña, which typically results in a more northerly storm track during winter months. Conversely, drier-than-average conditions are anticipated for the southern U.S., from the Southwest to the Southeast. <4> Major Hurricane Milton made landfall near Siesta Key, Florida, on the evening of October 9, 2024, as a powerful Category 3 storm with sustained winds of 120 mph. Prior to landfall, as the storm approached and tracked across the Florida peninsula from October 8–9, its outer bands generated a historic and deadly tornado outbreak. This event became the largest single-day tornado outbreak in state history, producing 46 confirmed tornadoes, with at least three reaching EF3 intensity. The hurricane also produced torrential rainfall, leading to widespread and, in some areas, historic flooding. While rainfall amounts generally ranged from 10 to 15 inches, some locations received over 18 inches, with one airport in St. Petersburg recording 18.54 inches in a single day. The storm, which had earlier been a Category 5 hurricane in the Gulf of Mexico, caused devastating storm surge along the coast and significant power outages affecting over 3 million customers. <5> On September 25, 2024, forecasters, including the National Hurricane Center, issued warnings for Hurricane Helene, predicting it would bring catastrophic flooding and life-threatening conditions to the southeastern United States. [7, 10, 22] The storm made landfall in Florida's Big Bend region on the evening of September 26, 2024, as a Category 4 hurricane before moving inland across Georgia and into the southern Appalachians on September 27. [8, 9, 17] The event was exacerbated by a prior stalled frontal system that had already saturated the ground. [8, 12] This led to record-breaking rainfall in western North Carolina, with some areas receiving 12 to over 20 inches of rain over a two-day period. [8, 12] The southern Blue Ridge mountains were severely impacted, with communities in western North Carolina and eastern Tennessee experiencing historic and devastating flooding, mudslides, and widespread power outages. [8, 24] The extensive flooding led to numerous fatalities and destroyed infrastructure, including homes, bridges, and roads, isolating many towns. [9, 23, 24] <6> On Sunday, August 18, 2024, a slow-moving front produced extreme rainfall and catastrophic flooding in the Northeast, primarily impacting southwestern Connecticut and Long Island, New York. [8] The National Weather Service in Omaha, Nebraska, issued a record 48 tornado warnings on one day of the storm. [14] An analysis by World Weather Attribution concluded that human-caused climate change made the extreme rainfall associated with this event 9% more intense and 40% more likely. [3] The study noted that abnormally warm Gulf of Mexico water temperatures, made 14 times more likely by climate change, fueled the storms. [3] <5> A forecast issued on May 5, 2025, predicted a multiday flood and severe weather event for the southern Plains and Gulf Coast, driven by an Omega blocking pattern. [1, 5, 6, 7] The most significant threat identified was the potential for major flash flooding in Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi, beginning the week of May 5, 2025. [5, 13] Subsequent reports on May 7 confirmed that severe weather, including softball-sized hail, had impacted Texas and Louisiana the previous day. [9] These storms led to ongoing flash flood threats and warnings, particularly for southeastern Louisiana, with predictions of rainfall totals possibly exceeding half a foot by the end of the week. A particularly intense gust, estimated between 110-120 MPH, was recorded in Cambria County where it destroyed a cellular antenna tower. The storm left a trail of extensive damage, including snapped trees, downed power lines, and damaged structures, with a significant portion of the damage concentrated between I-80 and US Route 22. [2] The system produced at least 63 confirmed tornadoes, with the most widespread activity occurring on April 2nd and a deadly EF3 tornado striking Selmer, Tennessee, on April 3rd. [4] Total rainfall accumulations exceeded 6 inches in many areas, with some locations in Kentucky and Tennessee reporting over a foot of rain. The NWS Weather Prediction Center anticipated 4–7 inches (100–180 mm) of precipitation over the Olympic Peninsula, Oregon, and the Northern California coast ranges. In response to the forecasted rainfall, the NWS Northwest River Forecast Center predicted that three gauges in Oregon could exceed a minor flood stage, with one potentially surpassing a moderate flood stage. [2] The forecast indicated that the Great Lakes and Ohio Valley regions would likely experience above-average precipitation. [3, 5] For the Great Lakes region, this was expected to lead to an improvement in drought conditions. [2, 3] Despite the forecast for increased precipitation in the Ohio Valley, a significantly reduced flood risk was anticipated due to well-below-average snowpack.
